section_summary: This section of the file covers diplomatic despatches, telegrams, and reports from late 1939 regarding Japanese domestic politics, foreign policy, and imperial expansion, as well as several earlier reference items from 1933-1938. Prominent topics include internal bureaucratic conflict within the Japanese Foreign Office over the proposed Ministry of Foreign Trade, the platform and political instability of Prime Minister Nobuyuki Abe's Cabinet, and extensive Japanese youth volunteer colonization efforts in Manchuria and northern China. Later materials document diplomatic discussions in Paris and Tokyo regarding Sino-Japanese hostilities, treaty relations with the United States, Soviet military preparations in the Far East, and contemporary press coverage of Japanese social and political tensions.

subfiles.about: Transmits a statement by a Japanese-speaking Chinese estimating Japanese government personalities and political-military factions.
subfiles.summary: Counselor of Embassy Frank P. Lockhart forwards an estimate prepared by a Japanese-speaking Chinese who recently returned from Tokyo regarding the personalities administering the Japanese Government. The document outlines major political groupings, including pro-Axis diplomats, leading financiers, the Minami-Terauchi military faction, and the Itagaki clique. It concludes with observations on the military extremists' drive toward a totalitarian wartime economy in Japan and their approach to the conflict in China.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2236 from Peiping: Estimate Made by a Chinese of Certain Japanese Officials in Japan

subfiles.about: Reports widespread dissension and resignations in the Japanese Foreign Office over the proposed transfer of the Commercial Bureau to a new Ministry of Foreign Trade.
subfiles.summary: Dooman reports Foreign Minister Nomura faces mass insubordination after agreeing to move the Commercial Bureau to a Ministry of Foreign Trade, weakening the Abe Cabinet and Vice Minister Tani.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 504 from Tokyo regarding Dissension in the Foreign Office over the Proposed Ministry of Foreign Trade

subfiles.about: Reports the compromise settlement of the conflict between the Japanese Cabinet and Foreign Office officials regarding the projected Trade Ministry.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that the Abe Cabinet yielded to insubordinate Foreign Office officials, agreeing to a compromise that retains trade negotiations, commercial attachés, and commercial protection under Foreign Office jurisdiction. Admiral Nomura rejected the resignations of over 100 officials, but the Japanese press severely condemned both the Cabinet and the diplomats for damaging state prestige. Press speculation suggests that while Nomura will remain, Vice Minister Tani will resign to assume responsibility, with Sotomatsu Kato considered the most likely successor.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 521 from Tokyo regarding Settlement of the Foreign Office Dispute

subfiles.about: Transmits and analyzes the five-point policy platform announced by the Cabinet of Premier Nobuyuki Abe, accompanied by Japanese press reactions.
subfiles.summary: Chargé Eugene H. Dooman transmits translations of the five-point policy platform announced by the Abe Cabinet, along with a Department of State summary memorandum and vernacular press clippings. The platform emphasizes settling the China Incident, assisting the creation of a new central Chinese regime under Wang Ching-wei, expanding productive power across Japan, Manchukuo, and China, enforcing economic and price controls under the National General Mobilization Law, and renovating administrative organs. The Japanese press received the declaration with skepticism and apathy, noting the lack of novelty and criticizing the Cabinet's substitution of the phrase 'new relations between Japan and China' for 'a new order in East Asia.'
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4139 from Tokyo: Platform Announced by the Cabinet of Premier Abe

subfiles.about: Reports that a movement has developed to retain Masayuki Tani as Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs, delaying expected diplomatic appointments.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports a counter-movement to keep Vice Minister Tani despite announced resignation; Kato, named successor, returns to Shanghai meanwhile.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 545 from Tokyo regarding Proposed Retention of Vice Minister Tani

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum noting that facts regarding the Japanese Mobilization Bill in Despatch No. 2815 have already appeared in the press.
subfiles.summary: Brief note that the facts in Despatch No. 2815 on the National Mobilization Bill have already been published in the press.
subfiles.title: Memorandum regarding Tokyo Despatch No. 2815 on the Mobilization Bill

subfiles.about: Details the internal crisis and bureaucratic background of Foreign Minister Nomura's dispute with Foreign Office officials over the projected Trade Ministry.
subfiles.summary: Chargé Dooman provides a detailed account of the rebellion in the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs sparked by the Cabinet Planning Board's draft plan for a Ministry of Foreign Trade. Foreign Minister Admiral Nomura approved the plan at a cabinet meeting without consulting his staff, breaking a prior promise to Commercial Bureau Director Shikao Matsushima and provoking Matsushima's resignation along with threats of mass resignations from hundreds of diplomats. Dooman notes that Foreign Office officials feared further loss of ministerial influence following the earlier transfer of China affairs to the Asia Board, and concludes that the dispute was primarily administrative rather than a fundamental clash over foreign policy.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4175 from Tokyo: Dissension in Foreign Office over Projected Trade Ministry

subfiles.about: Comprehensive voluntary report on the mobilization, training, and dispatch of Japanese youth volunteer workers to Manchuria, North China, and Mongolia during summer 1939.
subfiles.summary: Consul Louis H. Gourley at Kobe reports on the program sending over 11,000 Japanese youth volunteers aged 14 to 19 to the Asian continent during the summer of 1939 to perform farm work, road construction, building, and military support. The report describes their preliminary training at Uchihara in Ibaraki Prefecture, their distribution across major training camps in Manchuria, and the strategic settlement efforts in northeastern border areas like Tungan Province near Soviet territory. Gourley and attached documents review the history of the youth volunteer settlement scheme since 1934, long-range mass emigration plans, and the economic hurdles posed by wartime factory wages in Japan.
subfiles.title: Voluntary Report: Japanese Youth Volunteer Summer Workers on Continent of Asia

subfiles.about: Reports French diplomatic assessments of the instability of the Abe Government and inquiries regarding Japanese promises to reopen the Yangtze River.
subfiles.summary: Bullitt reports French Foreign Office information that the Abe Cabinet is shaky, with Wang Ching-wei's demands rising. Chauvel asks about US views and the Yangtze reopening promise.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 3021 from Paris regarding French Information on Japanese Government Instability

subfiles.about: Instruction from the Secretary of State authorizing repetition of telegram instructions to diplomatic missions.
subfiles.summary: Hull's Telegram No. 1556 to Paris on repeating instructions on Far Eastern developments to other posts.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1556 to Paris regarding Far Eastern Communications

subfiles.about: Provides U.S. views on the Abe Cabinet's prospects, Soviet-Japanese rapprochement, and the conditional Japanese reopening of the Yangtze River.
subfiles.summary: Hull tells Bullitt the US sees no immediate fall of the Abe Cabinet and no alarm at Soviet-Japanese rapprochement. The US stands on non-discrimination, not bargaining over the Yangtze.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1563 to Paris regarding U.S. Policy toward Japan and the Yangtze Reopening

subfiles.about: Reports French agreement with U.S. views on Japan and describes momentary Japanese contact with French Indochina border guards.
subfiles.summary: Bullitt reports the Quai d'Orsay's views on the Abe Government match American views; Japanese forces briefly touched French Indochina frontier guards before retreating.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 3037 from Paris regarding French Indochina Frontier and U.S.-French Policy Alignment

subfiles.about: Reports on a resolution signed by 250 Diet members demanding the resignation of the Abe Cabinet and discusses political discontent in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports 250 Diet members demanded Abe's resignation over economic regimentation and the China war. Observers see the Cabinet's fall as inevitable, but no strong successor is visible.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 713 from Tokyo regarding Diet Resolution Demanding Cabinet Resignation

subfiles.about: Reports Premier Abe's press conference rejecting resignation demands, defending economic controls, and discussing U.S.-Japanese treaty relations.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Abe rejected the Diet's demand, saying his Cabinet will settle the China incident and establish a Wang Ching-wei regime. He hopes for a modus vivendi on the expiring 1911 treaty.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 715 from Tokyo regarding Premier Abe's Rejection of Diet Demands

subfiles.about: Transmits intelligence from London regarding Soviet military preparations in Vladivostok, Japanese preparations in Northern Manchuria, and Japanese colonization plans in Abyssinia.
subfiles.summary: Batsell relays a London source: Maisky finds the Far East grave, Japan preparing northern Manchuria bases, Soviet submarines at Vladivostok, and a Japanese cotton concession in Abyssinia displeasing Italy.
subfiles.title: Letter from Walter R. Batsell to Robert F. Kelly regarding Russian-Japanese Military Situation

subfiles.about: Article by publisher Robert Cromie interpreting the February 26, 1936 military assassinations in Tokyo as an uprising of the Japanese masses against financial oligarchs.
subfiles.summary: Vancouver Sun, April 1, 1936: Robert Cromie calls the February 26 Incident social warfare by the masses and military against a financial oligarchy. Adjacent news columns cover unrelated matters.
subfiles.title: Newspaper Clipping from The Vancouver Sun: 'Japan's Masses And Ruling Clique In Social War'
